div.p: Absmct -Scheduling guarantees are essential in many real-time embedded computer systems. They can only be achieved by performing analysis of scheduling feasibility prior to run-time. This paper examines some issues related to this problem in the context of hardware architectures that are more complex than a single bus linking several processors. It raises questions about how well existing static scheduling and shedulability analysis techniques scale up to the larger systems that are likely to be in use in the future.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Static scheduling, also called pre-run-time scheduling, allows the timing behaviour of real-time computer systems to be guaranteed prior to execution. Static scheduling algorithms are based on characterizing, tasks in terms of parameters such as deadlines, intertask constraints, release times, and maximum computation time.

Computer science research has tended to emphasize dynamic scheduling, which includes factors such as fairness and priority to schedule tasks at run-time. There are many circumstances in which scheduling guarantees are required for safe operation, and so dynamic scheduling alone is inadequate.

Most research to date on static scheduling has neglected the effects of computer architecture and the number of resources being scheduled on the applicability of scheduling algorithms. In typical military and aerospace embedded systems being designed today, single processor systems are rare. More common is a single bus architecture supporting several processors. Often the main bus is replicated for fault tolerance, and there are secondaq buses for I/O. In future systems, it is expected that architectures involving clusters of processors will be common. Intercluster connections will be made through hierarchical buses or by a distributed network. Design choices will be based on maintainability, the need to maximize efficiency of communication, the ever increasing need for processing resources, and the need to support specialized requirements such as fault tolerance. Scheduling will have to include both processor and other resources. Communications links in particular will have to be scheduled.

Scheduling algorithms will have to be capable of handling hundreds of resources. It is not clear that currently available algorithms have this capability, but a natural decomposition of scheduling based on pre-assignment of tasks to specific architectural components may help to solve this problem. Many existing algorithms for multiresource scheduling assume that tasks can be freely allocated to any available resource, or, if resources are heterogeneous, it is only in the sense of some processors being faster than others. In reality, designers of embedded systems make allocation decisions for reasons such as replication (the Same fhctionality may be needed in more than one location for application specific reasons), uniqueness (e.g. a communication task can only run on a resource that can perform the communication), and fault tolerance (backup tasks must be on different processors from the tasks bemg backed up). This leads to additional constraints that must be respected by the scheduling algorithm.

The research described in this paper begins the extension of algorithms for static scheduling previously developed at RMC with the aim of covering the situations described above. Associated with this research is the creation of a sample hardware and software architecture obtained by abstracting from the hardware architecture and program task structure of a system currently in development. The motivation for such a sample architecture is to ensure the existence of a realistic test bed for verification of the scheduling algorithms.

The remainder of the paper is organized into the following sections: HRT scheduling background, specification and design methods for HRT systems, architectural issues, a sample architecture, a proposed static scheduling model, and conclusions

div.head: HRT SCHEDULING BACKGROUND
div.p: A definition of Hard Real-Time is that not only must all tasks be completed correctly, but they must be completed in a timely fashion. If a task fails to complete in a timely fashion the result could be catastrophic or fatal. At present most HRT systems are scheduled at run-time. These methods are getting more and more sophisticated (e.g. [14],[4],[13]), but they do not guarantee that all tasks will meet their deadlines.
Static scheduling or pre-run-time schedulability analysis is required to provide a guarantee that the timing constraints of all tasks are strictly observed at run-time.

div.head: Several techniques have been proposed for providing schedulability guarantees. A good overview of previous work is found in [20]; other work includes 19, IO].
div.p: Hard Real-Time systems require only a feasible schedule at run-time, not an optimal schedule. A non-optimized schedule does have the disadvantage that it provides less flexibility for any further expansiodmodification of the system. With a given set of resources and tasks to be scheduled, even finding a feasible schedule quickly becomes an NP-Hard problem [7]. By using heuristics, "-Hard problems can be solved in practice. A drawback with using heuristics is that it is possible to eliminate the only feasible solution. In at least some cases, in practice, heuristics are not needed, as the search space is small [2].

Work on pre-run-time scheduling at RMC began with the application of techniques developed in [19] to the multiprocessor computer of the F 18 [ 15, 161. [ 181 extends the techniques of [ 191 to the multiprocessor case. Tools implementing a number of other static scheduling algorithms have been developed at RMC [ l , 111. These algorithms were modified from their original forms to allow scheduling of heterogeneous resources. The tools allow visualization of algorithm behaviour and a performance comparison of heuristic algorithms versus algorithms that find optimal solutions. The algorithms handle non-preemptive task sets on both heterogeneous and homogeneous processor sets.

Hard Real-Time systems interact with their environment. The interaction takes place through sensor data input, device actuators, data acquisition devices, user interfaces, digital-to-analog converters and other means.

These devices have particular timing characteristics such as rise, setup and hold times, slew rate, and sampling frequency (periodic) or maximum rate of occurrence (aperiodic). Typically, most interaction is periodic. It is possible to convert an aperiodic task into a pseudo-periodic task on the basis of its maximum rate of occurrence. When the actual rate of occurrence is significantly lower than the maximum rate, this strategy is unattractive. The alternative is to use statistically based analysis, but very little work has been done in this direction. The present collection of methodologies is more diverse than it will eventually be, reflecting an immature state of the art. One of the indicators of immaturity is that there is a gap between the requirements level specification of timing behaviour and the schedulability analysis that is possible at the implementation level. Schedulability analysis can either be done implicitly through static scheduling algorithms as discussed in this paper or explicitly through the use of a programming language that supports the description of timing constraints. For example, Real-Time Euclid or PEARL can be used to construct predictable systems at the implementation stage 191.

div.head: SPECIFICATION AND DESIGN METHODS FOR HRT
SYSTEMS
div.p: If tasks and task timing are identified at design time, then static scheduling can be applied at that stage. Most software designers are still content just to produce a feasible system by whatever means they can, let alone an optimal one. This is not a reflection on their abilities, but it is a measure of the immaturity of the discipline, especially in terms of producing maintainable code that continues to satisfy timing requirements in a verifiable fashion as a system evolves. Since most designers design for run-time schedulers, it is extremely difficult and costly, both in time and money, to redesign or re-engineer a piece of HRT code that works. Static scheduling and schedulability analysis, on the other hand, offer the designer the chance to check the feasibility of the proposed system after each change

In the design as presented, the timings shown opposite each component are estimates of how long that component will take to execute. Estimates are given only for the main processor of each DPU. There is also some indication in the design documentation of what the individual timing requirements are for specific functions. Verification of timing behaviour will amount to comparison of actual execution times to estimates plus verification that those timing constraints specified between events are met. It would be useful to give more formal statements of timing requirements in terms of actual response times to particular events in order to reduce ambiguity and facilitate verification.
